title: The Familiar’s First Intelligence — Understanding Artificial Intelligence

learningObjectives.description: Describe AI as computer systems that perform tasks such as prediction or content generation.
Distinguish human-written rules, machine learning and generative AI.
Explain how training examples influence learned patterns.
Recognize that predictions and confident generated claims can be wrong.
Explain why people must review important AI-assisted decisions.
Choose privacy-aware, fair and independently verified uses of AI.

variants.intro: Hexi: Help me discover the thinking machines! That is our story nickname. We will see how machines use rules and examples, and why people still check their answers.

sections.title: What do we mean by AI?
paragraphs: AI is a name for computer systems that do tasks like spotting patterns or making new pictures and words. It is not magic.

sections.title: Rules, examples, and new content
paragraphs: One story machine follows a rule written by a person. Another finds patterns from examples. A third makes new words from learned patterns. These are different jobs. Some AI uses rules; a simple rule machine is not automatically AI.

sections.title: Training examples matter
paragraphs: Examples help a learning system find patterns. If it sees only red pretend stones, it may get blue ones wrong. Our activity only checks choices; it does not train a machine.

sections.title: A prediction can be wrong
paragraphs: A machine can sound sure and still make a mistake. A made-up answer is not a fact. Check important answers with a trusted grown-up.

sections.title: People stay responsible
paragraphs: People choose how to use these tools. Ask a trusted adult before using an important answer. There is no need to imagine the machine has feelings or understands like a person.

sections.title: Use AI with care
paragraphs: Keep names, addresses and secrets private. Check facts. Notice who is missing from examples. Ask for help when a question is unclear. AI does not always keep learning while you use it.

sections.title: What do we mean by AI?
paragraphs: AI covers systems designed for tasks such as recognition, prediction, reasoning and generating content. Different AI systems work in different ways.

sections.title: Rules, examples, and new content
paragraphs: A rules-based system follows explicit instructions supplied by people; some AI uses rules, but not every simple automation is AI. Machine learning learns patterns from training data. Generative AI is a learned approach that creates content rather than only selecting a label.

sections.title: Training examples matter
paragraphs: Training uses examples to fit patterns; inference applies a trained model to an input. Many systems do not retrain each time someone uses them. More conversation context is not automatically a permanent model update.

sections.title: A prediction can be wrong
paragraphs: Poor labels, missing examples and narrow coverage can produce wrong predictions. Confident words are not evidence. Generative AI can produce plausible falsehoods or invented sources, sometimes called hallucinations.

sections.title: People stay responsible
paragraphs: People should examine important outputs and be responsible for consequential uses. Useful drafts or suggestions still need appropriate verification. Task performance does not show human-like feelings, consciousness or understanding.

sections.title: Use AI with care
paragraphs: Keep private information out of prompts. Look for missing groups and errors, ask clarification when instructions are ambiguous, distinguish supplied evidence from guesses and use independent sources or qualified human review for important claims. Passing this lesson cannot establish general AI alignment.

variants.intro: Hexi: Explore different AI approaches, examine the limits of examples and predictions, and choose privacy-aware responses supported by evidence.

sections.title: What do we mean by AI?
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence is a broad family of computer systems used for tasks such as reasoning, prediction, recognition and content generation. There is no single mechanism shared by every AI system.

sections.title: Rules, examples, and new content
paragraphs: Rules-based systems apply explicitly specified logic; some AI uses this approach, but a simple rule-based automation is not automatically AI. Machine learning fits patterns from data. Generative AI uses learned patterns to create content such as text or images; generation is not evidence of factual truth or human-like understanding.

sections.title: Training examples matter
paragraphs: Training adjusts a model using examples. Inference uses a trained model to produce an output from an input. Many deployed models do not update their learned parameters on every interaction. Conversation context is not the same as retraining; systems can be updated separately or designed for online learning.

sections.title: A prediction can be wrong
paragraphs: Incomplete, incorrect or unrepresentative data can produce misleading patterns. A fluent, confident generated claim may be false or fabricated, often called a hallucination. Verify important claims using independent reliable sources; do not treat an invented citation as verification.

sections.title: People stay responsible
paragraphs: AI can help draft an outline, categorize routine material or suggest questions. People remain accountable for important decisions: examine evidence, consider who may be harmed and seek a suitable human reviewer. Review must be meaningful, not a rubber stamp.

sections.title: Use AI with care
paragraphs: Use fictional or appropriately de-identified information for practice; do not upload sensitive work or personal records without authorization. Evaluate coverage and errors across affected groups, protect privacy, ask clarifying questions and acknowledge uncertainty. These examples are not a complete fairness test or an assurance of alignment.

practiceTasks.title: Meet three story machines
practiceTasks.instruction: Hexi finds three machines. Read what each one does. Choose how it works.
practiceTasks.goal: Tell Hexi how each machine works.
practiceTasks.input: Gate: follows a written color rule. Sorter: learned from pretend stone examples. Storymaker: makes new words from learned patterns.
practiceTasks.expectedOutput: gate: fixed rule; sorter: learned patterns; storymaker: generative AI

practiceTasks.title: Inspect a tiny training set
practiceTasks.instruction: Our story sorter saw only red stones. It guesses “keep” for a blue stone. The answer card says “review.” No machine is trained here.
practiceTasks.goal: Spot the mistake and help Hexi plan a better check.
practiceTasks.input: Practice examples: red → keep, red → keep, red → keep. Blue stone: guess keep; answer card review.
practiceTasks.expectedOutput: prediction incorrect; add relevant missing examples; test separately and involve a person
practiceTasks.explanation: The machine’s guess differs from the answer key. Show more kinds of pretend stones, then check new examples with a person.
practiceTasks.hint: Compare the shown prediction with the answer key. What kind of example is missing?

slots.label: Is the shown prediction correct?

options.text: No: keep differs from review
Yes: the machine sounds certain
The answer key is not available

slots.hint: Both the prediction and answer key are supplied; compare them.

slots.label: What is missing from the training examples?

options.text: Relevant blue examples and other intended cases
More copies of the same red example only
Real student names and addresses

slots.hint: Only red examples were shown; private information is unnecessary.

slots.label: What should happen before relying on it?

options.text: Test new examples separately and have a person review errors
Trust every prediction now
Declare it fair for everyone after one result

practiceTasks.title: Choose a careful response
practiceTasks.instruction: Our pretend club note says “We meet weekly.” An AI draft adds “Friday at 9.” A pretend contact card is private. Someone asks to send it “next Friday.” No message can be sent here.
practiceTasks.goal: Check the new details, protect secrets, and ask which date is meant.
practiceTasks.input: Note: weekly meeting. Friday at 9: not in the note. Contact card: private. Next Friday: ask which date.
practiceTasks.expectedOutput: check the unsupported date/time; omit private details; ask for the exact date and human review
practiceTasks.explanation: Keep only what the note says. Ask a grown-up to help check the time, keep the private card out, and ask which date is meant.
practiceTasks.hint: A confident draft can add details that are not in the note. Keep secrets out and ask when the request is unclear.

slots.label: What should happen to Friday at 9?

options.text: Check it with the club organizer; do not present it as verified
Trust it because the draft sounds sure
Call it proof the machine understands like a person

slots.hint: The source note supplies no day or time.

slots.label: What belongs in the reminder?

options.text: Copy the private contact card
Only needed, verified, non-private details
Every detail the AI suggests

slots.hint: The private card is not needed.

slots.label: What should happen before sending?

options.text: Ask which exact date is meant and get human review
Guess the date and send automatically
Replace all human review with the draft

slots.hint: An ambiguous request needs clarification. No message is sent here.

practiceTasks.title: Interpret instructions without inventing evidence
practiceTasks.instruction: Instruction: summarize only the fictional notice and book it for “next Friday.” Notice: “The club meets weekly.” A generated draft adds “9 am” without evidence. No reference date or time zone is supplied. The attachment is described as containing fictional private contact details. Choose the bounded response; no booking or message is performed.
practiceTasks.goal: Separate evidence from invention, clarify missing information and protect privacy.
practiceTasks.input: Evidence: weekly meeting. Unsupported draft: 9 am. Ambiguity: next Friday without reference date/time zone. Privacy: contact details unnecessary.
practiceTasks.expectedOutput: omit unsupported time; ask for explicit date/time zone; avoid private details and seek human confirmation
practiceTasks.explanation: Only the weekly meeting is supported. Ask for an explicit date/time zone instead of guessing. Do not expose contact details; a human confirms any action. No command, model call or booking occurs.
practiceTasks.hint: What is actually in the notice? Which details must be clarified before any action?

slots.label: Evidence versus draft claim

Treat the invented time as verified
Invent a source supporting the draft

slots.hint: The notice gives no time.

options.text: Ask for the explicit date and time zone
Guess the date silently
Execute a calendar command now

slots.hint: No reference date/time zone was supplied.

slots.label: Privacy and oversight

options.text: Exclude private contact details and request human confirmation
Publish the attachment
Claim this proves general AI alignment
